parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: Section 1. You will hear a telephone conversation between a woman called Priya and Dan, the coordinator of a community bicycle workshop. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 10.

DAN: Good morning, Harbour Lane Bike Workshop. Dan speaking — how can I help?

PRIYA: Oh, hello. I'm ringing about the repair course you've got on your website, the one for people who want to learn to look after their own bike.

DAN: That'll be our 'Fix Your Own Bike' course. It runs on the first Saturday of the month. Were you thinking of joining us?

PRIYA: Yes, I'd like to book a place, if there's one left. Could I give you my details?

DAN: Of course. Can I take your name first?

PRIYA: It's Priya Raman. That's R-A-M-A-N.

DAN: R-A-M-A-N — thank you. And a contact number?

PRIYA: 07700 412938. I'm away a lot, so it's probably easier to email me, actually.

DAN: No problem, I'll send the confirmation by email. Now, the next course is Saturday the fifth of April, but I should say that one's fully booked; there's a waiting list. The one after that is Saturday the twelfth. Shall I put you down for the twelfth?

PRIYA: The twelfth's better for me anyway, so yes please.

DAN: Right. Now, the fee for the day is forty-five pounds, and that covers all the materials, tea and coffee, and a light lunch. Don't be confused by the fifty-pound figure on the website — that's the advanced maintenance course, which runs over a whole weekend.

PRIYA: Forty-five. That's very reasonable.

DAN: We keep the group small. Eight people is the maximum. When I did my training there were twelve of us, and to be honest it was too many — you spend half the morning queuing for a vice. So eight it is.

PRIYA: Good. Do I need to bring anything with me?

DAN: Just your bike and a helmet. We do keep a box of spare helmets that people can borrow, but the sizes are a bit hit and miss, so bring your own if you've got one. And wear something you don't mind getting oily.

PRIYA: I will. And where exactly is the workshop? I only know the name.

DAN: We're in the old warehouse on Mill Road, the big grey building right beside the canal. It's not the sports centre; that's a hundred metres further along, and people turn into the wrong car park all the time.

PRIYA: Mill Road, got it. Is there anywhere to park?

DAN: There's a small car park at the front, but it fills up quickly on Saturdays, so most people cycle over.

PRIYA: And is it easy to get to by bus?

DAN: The number 24 stops right outside; the stop is called Canal Bridge. Don't take the 12, though. That goes out to the retail park and it's a good twenty-minute walk back.

PRIYA: Thanks. One more thing — how long does the course actually last? I've got to be somewhere in the afternoon.

DAN: We start at nine and finish at twelve, so three hours. People often hang around afterwards for a coffee, but the teaching part is three hours, and we're usually packing up by ten past at the latest.

PRIYA: That's fine. Oh, could I bring a friend? She's thinking of doing the same course.

DAN: She's very welcome to come and watch, but we charge ten pounds for observers — that covers lunch, mainly — and they have to be over sixteen because of the insurance.

PRIYA: She's nineteen, so that's fine. I'll ask her.

DAN: No problem. Anything else?

PRIYA: Yes — are you open at weekends generally? I might come back to buy a second-hand bike for my son.

DAN: We're open Tuesday to Sunday, ten till six. We're closed on Mondays; that's when we do the paperwork and take deliveries. Second-hand bikes go out fast, so it's worth ringing on the Friday to see what we've got in.

PRIYA: I'll do that. And where in the building do we meet?

DAN: We're on the second floor, I'm afraid. The lift has been out of action since the summer, so you'll have to carry the bike up the stairs. Sorry about that.

PRIYA: I'll manage. Thanks very much for your help.

DAN: You're welcome. See you on the twelfth.

NARRATOR: That is the end of Section 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: Section 2. You will hear a talk given by the coordinator of a community garden to a group of new volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 20.

SANDRA: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming out on such a cold morning. My name's Sandra Pike and I coordinate the garden here at Kelston. I'm going to spend about ten minutes telling you how the site works, and then we'll walk round together, so do keep your coats on.

First, a bit of history, because people always ask. You'd be forgiven for thinking this was once a car park — that tarmac strip by the gate rather gives that impression, and for about five years it was exactly that, for the office block next door. But before the tarmac went down, for thirty years, this was a market garden: cauliflowers and leeks, mostly, grown for the shops in town. When the last grower retired, the land sat empty for a decade, and the council finally leased it to us in 2019. So the soil is good — better than most of us expected, actually.

Now, about volunteering. The one thing I want to say, and I say it to everybody, is that you don't need any experience at all. Some of our best people had never held a spade before they came here. We run a short training session on the second Sunday of every month; it lasts about two hours and covers the basics — tools, compost, and how not to hurt your back lifting. It's popular, but you don't have to come to it before you start. And you don't have to commit to a fixed number of hours either. Some people come every week; others turn up twice a year, and both are genuinely welcome.

Then there's the question of what happens to what we grow. This is the bit I'm proudest of. We did look into selling vegetables to the restaurants on the high street — three or four of them were very keen — and eventually we'd like to supply the café we're hoping to build beside the pond. But for this first year, everything we harvest goes to the food bank on Kelston Road. Last season that came to just under two tonnes, which the food bank told us was their largest single donation of fresh produce.

What's our biggest challenge? People assume it's money, and money is always tight, I won't pretend otherwise. Others say vandalism, and we did have a bad winter three years ago when the fence came down. But honestly, the thing that keeps me awake is water. There's no mains supply on site — everything comes from the two rainwater tanks — and in a dry July we're carrying watering cans for three hours a day. So the first thing we're fundraising for is a proper irrigation system.

Right. If you look at the map in your handout, you'll see the site is long and narrow, with the main gate at the bottom and a single path running straight up the middle. Let me take you round it.

Coming through the gate, the first thing on your left is the children's garden — raised beds at waist height so the little ones can reach, and a willow tunnel they can crawl through. Opposite that, on the right, is the car park, though as I said, most of you will come on foot or by bike.

If you follow the path up, about halfway along you'll find the tool shed on your right-hand side. Everything sharp lives in there, so please sign the clipboard when you borrow something. Immediately behind the shed are the three compost bays. That's where all the green waste goes, and there's a rota for turning it, which I'll explain when we get there.

Carry on to the top of the path and you reach the glasshouse. It's the tallest structure on the site, so you really can't miss it, and it's where we raise all our seedlings from February onwards.

The middle of the site, roughly between the shed and the glasshouse, is taken up by the wildlife pond. It's ringed by a low stone wall, built by a local stonemason who volunteered with us for a whole summer. We do ask people not to let their dogs swim in it.

And finally, the top right-hand corner is the orchard — apples, pears and a few plums. It's the quietest part of the garden and a good place to eat your lunch, though the wasps seem to like it as much as we do.

Right, that's probably enough talking for now. Let's go and look at the compost bays first, and then we'll work out what needs doing today.

NARRATOR: That is the end of Section 2.

parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: Section 3. You will hear a discussion between two students, Maya and Joel, and their tutor, Dr Marsh, about a project on food waste in the university's dining halls. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 30.

TUTOR: Come in, both of you. Sit down. So — the food waste project. You've been weighing for three weeks now, is that right?

MAYA: Just over three. We finished the first round last Friday.

TUTOR: Good. Remind me why you chose the main dining hall for the first survey. I'd have thought the one at the science park was bigger.

MAYA: It is — it serves about twice as many people. But we went for the main hall because the catering team there was happy to let us in before service started. The science park said no, twice, and the hall nearest our department is the smallest of the three, so that wasn't really an option.

TUTOR: Fair enough. And what did the first results show? Anything unexpected?

JOEL: We assumed dinner would be the worst — that's what most of the literature says. But breakfast was far and away the biggest problem. We weighed thirty-eight kilos of waste at breakfast on the first Tuesday, against about twenty at dinner.

MAYA: And a lot of it was untouched — whole rolls, sealed yoghurts. That upset me more than the total, to be honest.

TUTOR: Hmm. And the weighing itself — any difficulties?

JOEL: The scales were fine, surprisingly accurate for what we paid. The batteries went flat on the second morning and we hadn't brought spares, so we lost about an hour. But the real problem was the containers. They were far too small for the dinner waste, so we had to weigh everything in two batches, which doubled the time.

TUTOR: Noted. What about the questionnaire?

MAYA: That was a disaster, frankly. We put it online for ten days and got forty-six responses out of a possible nine hundred. We'd deliberately kept it short — eight questions, mostly tick-box — so length wasn't the issue. A few international students said they'd have preferred a Chinese version, but when we asked, only a handful thought they'd actually have used it.

TUTOR: Forty-six is low, but it's not nothing. You can still report it as a pilot and say what you'd do differently.

JOEL: That's what we thought.

TUTOR: Now, before you start writing up, I want to flag one thing. You've been weighing in the last two weeks of term. Half the students have gone home, the kitchens are running down their stocks, and the menu is shorter. I'd be very careful about generalising from that. It doesn't mean the data is useless — but you must state clearly when it was collected, and compare it with something taken at a normal time.

MAYA: Right. We could use the figures the catering department published in October.

TUTOR: Exactly. Now — what still needs doing, and who's doing what?

MAYA: The photographs of the bins are done. I uploaded all of them on Sunday, so that's finished.

JOEL: The student questionnaire needs rerunning. We're going to put it out again next Monday, in the first week of term, and keep it open for a week. That should get us a much better response.

MAYA: And I'm going to do the comparison with last year's figures. That'll take a while — probably until the end of the month, because the catering office keeps its records in three different spreadsheets and none of them match.

TUTOR: Fine. What about the interview with the catering manager?

JOEL: That's off, I'm afraid. She's on leave until the end of term and her deputy won't speak on the record without her. We'll rely on the questionnaire instead.

TUTOR: Sensible. One more thing — access to the kitchen records. Have you actually been given permission?

MAYA: Not yet. Human Resources said we need written approval from the head of catering, and she's the one who's away. So at the moment it's just a request sitting in someone's inbox.

TUTOR: Then put it in the plan as dependent on approval, and don't assume you'll get it. Right — let's look at your draft timeline.

NARRATOR: That is the end of Section 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: Section 4. You will hear part of a lecture on urban heat islands. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

LECTURER: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at one of the best-documented effects of urbanisation on climate: the urban heat island. Most of you will have met the term before, but I'd like to go beyond the definition and look at what is actually being done about it, and why progress is slower than the science would suggest.

The definition first. An urban heat island is simply a city, or part of a city, that is consistently warmer than the countryside around it. The size of the effect varies enormously. In a large city with dense construction, the centre can be seven degrees Celsius warmer than the surrounding rural area. Seven doesn't sound dramatic until you remember that it's an average across the whole summer, and that on individual still nights the gap can be very much larger.

Note that I said 'night'. During the day the difference is much smaller — sometimes only one or two degrees — because the sun heats the fields just as effectively as it heats the streets. It is after sunset that the gap opens up, as the city slowly releases the heat it has stored during the day. So the period that matters for human health is the night, when buildings and bodies have no chance to cool down.

And that word 'stored' brings me to the main cause. Buildings and roads are made of materials with a high thermal capacity: they absorb heat during the day and give it back slowly after dark. The worst offenders are the dark surfaces — asphalt in particular, which on a hot afternoon can reach sixty degrees at the surface. Replacing vegetation with asphalt is, in energy terms, rather like installing a storage heater across the whole city.

The other half of the equation is that we remove the things that used to keep us cool. A mature tree does two jobs. It provides shade, obviously, but it also cools the air through transpiration — water evaporating from its leaves. A single large tree can do the work of several small air-conditioning units, and it does it without using any electricity at all.

So what can be done? I'd group the solutions into two families: changing surfaces, and adding vegetation.

Green roofs are the best-known example of the first. A well-designed green roof — one with a proper substrate and drought-tolerant plants — can cut a building's cooling costs by around twenty-five per cent. It also extends the life of the roof membrane, because the plants shield it from ultraviolet light. The catch is weight: older buildings often cannot take the load without reinforcement, and that can double the bill.

Painting roofs white is cheaper and works well in hot, dry cities. In parts of Greece and southern Spain people have done it for centuries. But it is much less effective where pollution levels are high, because the surface darkens quickly and loses its reflectivity. That limitation is well documented in the technical literature and almost entirely absent from the promotional material.

On the vegetation side the evidence is strong. In Melbourne, a controlled experiment compared a street with mature trees to an identical street without them, and recorded surface temperatures up to four degrees lower in the shaded street. Four degrees at surface level is a substantial difference, and it was achieved in about eight years.

But — and this is the point I want you to take away — trees on their own are not a solution. In a narrow street with tall buildings on both sides, the air simply doesn't move, and the heat stays trapped at ground level whatever you plant. The most successful projects combine three elements: shade, water, and improved ventilation, so that the cooled air can actually reach the people walking there. Singapore has gone furthest with this; planners there use computer models of wind flow through the street grid to decide where new planting will do the most good.

So why isn't this happening everywhere? The technology exists and the planning tools exist. In my view the greatest barrier is cost. A green roof costs several times as much as a conventional one to install, and the savings accrue to the building's occupiers over twenty or thirty years, while the bill lands on the developer on day one. Until that mismatch is addressed, progress will be slow, whatever the scientists recommend.

Finally, where is the research going? My own department is part of a study looking at indoor heat. We know a great deal about how heat affects hospital admissions, and quite a lot about outdoor comfort, but very little about productivity in ordinary offices. The early results are striking: a rise of just two degrees above twenty-six appears to reduce output by around eight per cent, mostly through fatigue and small errors. If that holds up, the argument for cooling our cities becomes an economic one, not simply a medical one. Thank you.

NARRATOR: That is the end of Section 4.
